Anyone with that trunk history can then fetch the branch using the same pack.
Several of these improvements are already in upstream Git, and many others in our public repository. We’re continuing to work with the Git community to make these improvements useful beyond Pando. You can follow that work in our public patch tracker(opens in a new window).
By rethinking conventional wisdom on how to scale Git repositories, Pando enables us to scale our monorepo without changing the Git workflows our engineers and agents already use. In our monorepo, Pando has unlocked a greater degree of parallelism, improved merge reliability, and reduced the time it takes to publish code changes. Beyond our monorepo, we’re also exploring other uses for Pando within OpenAI, including workloads where large numbers of agents need to collaborate on a shared Git repository.
As engineers and agents produce more software, more teams beyond OpenAI will encounter the limits we hit in source control. We’re currently exploring ways to share the technology that makes Pando possible with our users.
Pando builds on two decades of experience from users and operators of Git repositories. We’ll continue to develop Pando while working with the open-source Git community to share any improvements that benefit Git users more broadly.

articles.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI
articles.body:
Scaling Git at OpenAI
Building agentic-scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.
Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.
We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.
We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.
Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.
Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.
These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.
Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.
We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git(opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.
Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.
First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.
Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.
These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.
Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references.
A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.
Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.
Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.
Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.
In Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.
A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.
Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing reference updates, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.
While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.
In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.
To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.
Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.
Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.
In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.
Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The round-trip time for a successful compare-and-swap limits how often the repository can publish a new manifest. A low-latency blob store makes this step fast. Batching lets one manifest update several refs at the same time, at the cost of queueing updates and increasing latency.
The blob store can receive packfiles in parallel, but updates to the shared manifest still compete with one another. Increasing the blob store’s capacity alone doesn’t resolve that bottleneck. Each replica still needs to read and index packs from the blob store before it can serve them locally. If incoming writes outpace that work, replicas fall behind and clients wait longer to fetch newly pushed commits.
That brings us to Pando. Pando is a new architecture for serving Git repositories with the goal of scaling to many clients pushing simultaneously. Here’s how it works:
Prior to developing Pando, we had a hunch that we could meet our requirements without compromising on Git, but we did need to compromise on some of the things that most Git systems assume to be requirements:
- Repository-wide consistency: Providing a consistent, point-in-time snapshot of all refs requires coordination across the repository. In a system that orders all ref updates together, pushes to unrelated branches contend on a single coordination point.
- Unique packfiles for every client: If two clients with different local histories fetch the same branch, the server may need to generate a different pack for each to avoid sending objects they already have. Creating these responses costs CPU and disk I/O, making it difficult to scale to high volumes of readers.
Instead, Pando provides a relaxed consistency model (causal consistency) to scale writes, and reuses packfiles to scale reads.
When a client pushes to a branch, Pando stores the incoming packfile as an immutable blob in a blob store. Each time the branch moves, Pando records a ref version containing the new tip, the pack that supplied it, and any earlier ref versions the pack depends on in a metadata store. Both the blob store and metadata store are horizontally scalable.
Fetching a commit or reference from Pando requires replaying a set of ref versions (packfiles) to the client, reconstructing the state of the client that created the ref version being fetched. This provides a weaker form of consistency across the entire repository, while providing serializability for updates to individual refs. Clients only conflict when pushing to the same ref simultaneously. A client reading several branches cannot assume those reads describe a single point in time across the repository.
This is a form of causal consistency. In order to fetch a reference, the reader observes the history of the writer that produced it. During a push, Pando controls what shared history the client and server agree on, ensuring clients produce more easily shared packfiles.

Concretely, suppose that branches foo and bar are both updated during the negotiation of a full clone. During the negotiation, one client may observe foo at version 1 and bar at version 2, while another client observes foo at version 2 and bar at version 1. In practice, users and agents are agnostic to the global ordering of ref updates, and instead depend on the order of updates to a single reference.

The simulation models hardware ranging from commodity to premium virtual machines and blob storage systems. In this simulation, we’ve relaxed repository-wide consistency for three-phase commit.
The modeled three-phase commit system shows significantly greater write latency under load as their disks saturate; meanwhile, write-ahead log systems show significantly greater read latency for the same reason, as servers struggle to keep up with reading from the journal. In both real world testing on our monorepo and in this simulation, Pando supports many thousands of clients able to push concurrently without impacting performance under load.
On handling a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile while streaming it to blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. When a client begins a fetch Pando selects the stored packs the reader needs, and the reader downloads them. No server needs to apply packfiles to a local repository or perform costly unpack and packing operations. Because these servers primarily perform negotiation and packfile selection, Pando servers can run on commodity hardware.
This allows Pando to scale to the limits of clients, the network between clients and Pando, and the blob storage service. With enough capacity, clients working on independent branches can each transfer packs as fast as their own connection allows. To serve more clients at that rate, we can add Pando servers and scale the metadata store and blob store alongside them.
Pushing and Fetching a Branch in Pando
Pando stores the writer’s packfile in blob storage and records the ref version in metadata service. On fetch, Pando selects the packs the reader needs, and Express serves them.
An agent edits files and creates a commit locally and runs git push, which creates a packfile of those changes to update a branch. Pando receives the pack and streams it to blob storage. After validating the incoming push with a single pass decode, Pando uses a multi-key transaction to record a ref version in our metadata store and atomically update the ref pointer. This enables Pando to provide “read-your-own-write” consistency. This entire write operation requires \(O(1)\) metadata reads and writes.
When another client fetches the branch, Pando selects a set of stored packs using the history the client already has. This operation requires \(O(\log \Delta)\) metadata reads, \(\Delta\) being the shortest distance in ref versions between what the client has and what the client wants. The server returns packfile URIs, and the client downloads them through a service, Express, that stores packfiles in regional caches.

When a client pushes, a conventional Git server is like a poker player showing all of its cards, revealing to the client every branch it has. The client then gathers the commits, trees, and blobs to create a packfile that excludes objects it knows the server already has.
Advertising more refs can make the push smaller. It can also make the pack harder to reuse, because another client may be missing objects the writer left out.
Pando takes a different approach. Instead of showing its full hand, it only advertises a select set of branches to the client. This is done for two reasons:

- By providing only a subset of the refs to the client, the client will generate a pack that depends only on what the server explicitly allows the client to exclude. Each of those ref versions links to a packfile previously received by Pando. The server uses this to solve for what the client needs, selecting the packfiles that cover the set of objects the client needs.
Planning fetches in Pando
Pando compares what a client has with what it wants, then selects the stored packfiles needed—including any missing branch dependencies.

In our monorepo, Pando has unlocked a greater degree of parallelism, improved merge reliability, and reduced the time it takes to publish code changes. Beyond our monorepo, we’re also exploring other uses for Pando within OpenAI, including workloads where large numbers of agents need to collaborate on a shared Git repository.
As engineers and agents produce more software, more teams beyond OpenAI will encounter the limits we hit in source control. We’re currently exploring ways to share the technology that makes Pando possible with our users.
Pando builds on two decades of experience from users and operators of Git repositories. We’ll continue to develop Pando while working with the open-source Git community to share any improvements that benefit Git users more broadly.

articles.title: Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit By Second Suspected Cyberattack
articles.body:
Supermarket Freezers Across Europe Hit By Second Suspected Cyberattack (theguardian.com) 91
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France. Sweden's Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of its stores had been affected, while ICA said it was "aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems".
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last month reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands, said an "IT incident" had hit fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg. A company spokesperson, Sarah De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated. Belgium's Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets. "We started mobilizing technicians at 1am," Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. "We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid."

articles.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
articles.body:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S., Amit Sahai, and Jie Xue. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself.
There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us.
While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so.
The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order.
The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge.
Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view.
The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else?
Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves.
Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for.
From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine.
The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life.
This may sound like asking us all to become saints. Insofar as it asks us to grow in virtue and relinquish our attachment to our own importance, that impression is not far from the truth. But virtue is not something to cultivate for the admiration of others. It is necessary for genuine joy, even in our work. The satisfaction of solving a difficult problem or winning a prize can be fleeting when it rests on our standing relative to others. The joy of understanding is different. Something previously obscure becomes clear, and we recognize a beauty that does not diminish when someone else discovers it first. We can share this joy without depriving anyone of it. Growing in virtue allows us to experience it more fully, free from the need to establish our own importance.
This perspective may also help reconcile two positions within the mathematical community regarding AI. Some are comfortable with or even enthusiastic about using AI, but wish to develop appropriate processes and principles for its use. Others prefer not to use AI at all. Both positions have their merits. Egoless mathematics offers a way of reconciling them by introducing a higher consideration: both approaches can reflect the same underlying commitment to mathematical truth, regardless of how we choose to pursue it. Our aim here is not to settle particular questions of policy, but to develop a higher-level perspective that can guide our deliberations and ultimately our actions.
Seen in this light, we need not be afraid of what AI may achieve in mathematics. Mathematics was beautiful before any of us were born, and it will remain beautiful long after we are gone. Its worth does not depend on our accomplishments, nor does our joy in understanding it have to depend on being the ones who make the discoveries. Our purpose rests on our willingness to let truth govern what we seek and what we become.
We, the authors of this essay, are still far from having attained such egolessness. Nevertheless, we recognize it as an ideal toward which we wish to strive.
We conclude with a thought experiment. Ramanujan is reported to have said, “An equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God” (Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity, 1992). If he were alive today, witnessing the advances of AI in mathematics, would he be perturbed by what they might mean for his purpose as a mathematician?

articles.title: Open-Source 5G Ran Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
articles.body:
Computer Science > Networking and Internet Architecture
  [Submitted on 26 Aug 2026]
Title:Open-Source 5G RAN Platforms: A Dual Perspective on Performance and Capabilities
View PDF
            Abstract:Open-source implementations of the fifth generation (5G) Radio Access Network (RAN), such as OpenAirInterface (OAI) and srsRAN, have become increasingly relevant for industry and academic research, rapid prototyping, and low-cost private 5G deployments. The state of the art presents different evaluation scenarios for both platforms; however, these are often limited to individual testbed evaluations, end-to-end studies, or partial comparisons between them. In particular, there is a lack of evaluations considering different Software-Defined Radios (SDRs), RAN configurations, user applications, and numbers of real UEs. To address this gap, this paper presents a comparative evaluation of OAI and srsRAN. The study includes a qualitative assessment of supported features and deployment flexibility, followed by a quantitative performance analysis covering radio resource control setup procedures, compliance with theoretical data rates, and real application workloads with diverse quality of service requirements. Specifically, we consider Video on Demand (VoD) for data rate evaluation, Live Streaming (LS) and Cloud Gaming (CG) as latency-sensitive applications. These workloads provide a comprehensive view of each platform capability.

articles.title: Technofeudalism
articles.body:
Technofeudalism
Technofeudalism is a modern economic system where big technology companies have power similar to feudal lords in the past. Instead of land, these companies control digital platforms, data, and online markets. People and smaller businesses rely on these platforms, just like peasants once relied on feudal lords for land and protection.
Origins of the idea
[edit]
As a subject technofeudalism sits at the intersection of two subject areas, Information technology and Economics, and the concept has cropped up independently within both disciplines.
In Information Technology area Bruce Schneier wrote an article in November 2012 entitled "When It Comes to Security, We're Back to Feudalism"[1], which was published in Wired Magazine, another in December 2012 entitled "Feudal Security"[2], and another "You Have No Control Over Security on the Feudal Internet"[3] for Harvard Business Review in June 2013. Since then the term has entered the vocabulary of sites such as Slashdot.
Within Economics the concept of technofeudalism was described in an article[4] by Marina Gorbis of the Institute for the Future in 2010 and has been developed by several thinkers who argue that digital capitalism is shifting toward a new kind of economic control. While the term "technofeudalism" was later popularised by Durand (2020) and Varoufakis (2023), its conceptual roots can be traced to Kostakis and Bauwens, whose Network Society and Future Scenarios for a Collaborative Economy (2014) described "netarchical capitalism" as a "new-feudal form of cognitive capitalism"[5] in which centralised platforms enable user cooperation but appropriate all monetised exchange value, leaving the actual creators of value unrewarded. One of the most well-known voices on this topic is Yanis Varoufakis, an economist and former Greek finance minister. He argues that companies like Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Apple do not simply compete in markets—they own and control them, just like feudal lords controlled land in the Middle Ages.
French philosopher Cédric Durand also explores this idea in his book Technoféodalisme: Critique de l’économie numérique (2020), where he describes how digital platforms extract wealth from users, workers, and businesses without true competition. He claims that today’s economy is no longer based on traditional capitalism, where businesses compete, but on a system where a few tech giants rule over digital space.
These thinkers believe that rather than creating a free and open Internet, digital platforms have built a system where power is concentrated in the hands of a few, making it harder for smaller players to succeed.
Key features
[edit]
Technofeudalism is so called because users of the term perceive similarities between present-day technological systems and medieval feudal systems:
- Control over platforms – Large companies own and manage platforms like social media, e-commerce, and cloud computing, deciding who can participate.[6]
- Dependence on Big Tech – Businesses and workers must follow platform rules to earn money, similar to how peasants depended on lords.[7]
- Data ownership – Tech companies collect and use personal data, which gives them more power over users.[8]
- Limited competition – A few companies dominate entire industries, making it hard for smaller businesses to compete.[9]
See also
[edit]
References
[edit]
- ↑ Schneier, Bruce (2012-09-26). "When It Comes to Security, We're Back to Feudalism". Schneier on Security.
- ↑ Schneier, Bruce (2012-12-03). "Feudal Security". Schneier on Security.
- ↑ Schneier, Bruce (2013-06-06). "You Have No Control Over Security on the Feudal Internet". Schneier on Security.
- ↑ Gorbin, Marina (2010-09-01). "Ain't Gonna Work on Arianna's Farm No More". Institute for the Future.
- ↑ Kostakis, Vasilis; Bauwens, Michel (2014). Network Society and Future Scenarios for a Collaborative Economy. London: Palgrave Pivot. p. 23. doi:10.1057/9781137406897. OL 26384680M.
- ↑ Taghizade, Elgun; Ahmadov, Elchin (2025). "Techno Feudalism and the New Global Power Struggle: Echoes of a Digital Cold War". International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science. 9 (2): 1150–1151. doi:10.47772/IJRISS.2025.9020093. ISSN 2454-6186. Today, instead of land, technology companies like Amazon, Google, Facebook, and others hold control over vast digital infrastructures, data, and online platforms, positioning themselves as the new 'lords' of the digital realm. ...Under techno-feudalism, cloud capital functions much the same way as digital 'land' in creating virtual domains or 'digital fiefdoms,' such as Amazon.com. In those fiefdoms, platform owners not only extract value from the consumers but also the producers by imposing fees, which are similar to the ground rent of feudal times.
- ↑ Taghizade & Ahmadov (2025): 1151. "These platforms become so essential to modern life—much like utilities such as electricity or telecoms—that societies become dependent on them, making it nearly impossible to function without their services. This dependence gives tech companies immense power, much like feudal lords once held over land and resources."

articles.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
articles.body:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The news was announced via a press release sent out via Apple in India, but the update has not yet rolled out in the U.S. market as of this morning.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and the visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning, too.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards).
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.
Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.
Post updated to indicate that the updates have not yet rolled out in the U.S.

articles.title: I Read the Clankers' Code
articles.body:
I Read The Clankers' Code
  you shouldn’t look at the code, let the clanker do its thing
My name is attached to the PR, and I’m getting called at night when shit breaks. That, and I joined this whole endeavour because I actually quite like the code, and I’m actually curious to see it no matter who or what wrote it. So I’m gonna review it.
Admittedly, if I’m building a toy that I am the only user of, and don’t want to invest time into, I’ll ask a clanker to do it by itself. And I certainly won’t put my pristine, delicate little hands into the Rube Goldberg-esque pile of confusion that results of the cursed dreams that are what it thought I was asking for.
For everything else, I wanna see the code.
I get a lot of pride from the quality of my engineering[^5], what’s commonly called “my craft”. It’s part of my identity. Finding a solution that balances simplicity, reliability, security, cost, performance, maintainability, etc. I hate it when I break shit in prod. It’s a personal failure, I feel shame, it’s like a dirty spot on my reputation. I hate it when I ship shit, stuff that doesn’t work. And I hate it when someone else’s stuff breaks, and my big ugly face is attached to their PR with a dumb “👍 LGTM” next to it. When someone gets woken up because I fucked up some piece of software, I lose sleep myself. That’s the worst feeling.
This approach is incompatible with blindly trusting code written by a clanker. The code might be functional 95% of the time1. It might be decent, it might even be better than you’d have done. But 95% ain’t 100%. It misses things. It doesn’t have any curiosity. It doesn’t learn things like a human. It doesn’t stop and ask. It has a limited context window. Its entire training is maximizing a score. Its only goal is to complete the task: like a little puppy in training, it produces onto your feet a half-chewed, full-of-spit thing, that will somewhat match the prompt you gave it. Then it happily wags its tail, looking at you with googly eyes: “see, I did the thing, will you love me know?”. The larger the code base you work on, the higher the chance it’s going to introduce garbage. And then it compounds, building on the horrors that came out of its older, less sophisticated brethren.
Oh it writes code fast! It writes much, much faster than me. And more often than not (after reviews), its code is better than what I’d have done myself. And it gets there in a fraction of the time. It’s helpful. It’s a cool tool. I’m not saying “don’t use it”. I’m saying: as long as your name is on the PR, and your pager is in the on-call rotation, you own the code it builds, and you should read and understand it.
At this stage we’ve all got battle stories of that one time a clanker fucked up in an uniquely explosive and spectacular way. You’d let it roam free a little too long and it went crazy. Optimizations that are removing life-support level components. “Don’t touch this” bits of code touched to oblivion. Libraries pulled in carelessly. Features that it invents along the way. Unit tests altered to pass. Tons of code added to cover edge-cases that can’t be reached. And the code. Have you looked at the code? Code that is only built by addition. Thousands upon thousands upon thousands of task-specific unit-tests giving you 100% coverage of the wrong conditions. Re-implementation of functions implemented 14 times already. Redundancy all over the place. Useless comments over every single line of code. Alexandrian libraries worth of incorrect documentation that no-one will ever read. Then it breaks, you ask it why, and it bullshits some form of root cause analysis that makes no sense, with the conviction of a 4y old asserting that blue dogs do in fact exist.
Ask another agent to review the first agent’s code: more tests. More edge cases. Had you thought about what would happen if a Higgs boson flips that bit at that very moment? Ask to check the performance: you’re perfectly right, I forgot about that, let me add more code to add performance. If you let a clanker roam freely in your codebase, that’s what it’ll do. It’s often not as dramatic. Often it’s simpler issues. It mainly works by addition, and always limited to the immediate task at end: Let me add code. Write more code. Code here, code there, code everywhere. All of that amounts to garbage. And then it builds on top of that garbage.
But you don’t care about code quality anymore right. Since only clankers touch it, right? I do. Since I have to review the code, as I just said. I can’t properly do that if the code becomes a hot mess that I don’t understand anymore, I can’t let code quality slip.
  Ok but that sounds like a user issue: you’re bad at prompting and you’re putting it on the LLM.
Shit, I forgot to add you're a distinguished principal 10x engineermaxxer who's unfailable, make no mistakes and double-check your shit. All  those problems I’ve had with clankers might be patchable with mountains of carefully crafted prompts2. Maybe that’s what will differentiate developers in the future: each with their secret blend of sauce and spices that make their clanker the best clanker. I’m just an old, sour geezer. I’ve been paid for my code for 20 years, and I’m pretty good at it. Maybe I’ve earned a bit of credit to argue that I’ve made an earnest effort to insert that TOOL into my toolchain, and my conclusion at the moment is: the thing has been there for a couple of years, and it has given me reasons not to trust it blindly.
Secret herbs and spices don’t cut it when it comes to engineering. We need formalized processes, and proven, repeatable control mechanisms to enforce the quality of whatever is coming out of these tools. These do not exist yet. They might emerge one day, but they have not yet3. Until then, I won’t just lay into it blindly. If you consider yourself a software engineer, you should probably give it a minute too.
In my experience, no amount of system prompt, CLANKER.md instructions, re-iterations, reviews by other models, threats, or psychological manipulation seem to get clankers to reliably fix their behaviour. And that’s what really drives me nuts: when that particularly stubborn junior dev does the same mistake for the 3rd time, you get coachy for a minute, make sure they learn, and that actually helps them level up. Clankers don’t learn. They can’t, because the underlying technology cannot learn4. You can inject instructions in their context window. They will consider said instructions in evaluation if you’re lucky and then context will grow a little, and they’ll proceed to ignore whatever you said, preferring what’s baked in their weights. Maybe it will get better at some point. We’re not there yet.
When have curiosity and scrutiny become a bad thing? If you ask me to take the responsibility for code the clankers wrote, I need to review that code. And don’t tell anyone, but sometimes I even write it.
Notes
- I’m being generous there, don’t quote me on stats. ↩
- Doubt it. ↩
- And it might even be one of the most interesting things to work on in that clanker craze. ↩
- One could even argue that the proper of intelligence is to learn and adapt, and that LLMs should therefore be disqualified of being called Intelligence, artificial or not. But I’m not here to argue on marketing terminology. ↩

articles.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
articles.body:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.
On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.
“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.
He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”
As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.
For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”
Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.
“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”
But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

articles.title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
articles.body:
SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
The team directly observed a unique property in an altermagnetic candidate material, delivering key evidence of a new phase of magnetism first postulated in 2022.
Key takeaways:
- The scientific case for a third type of magnetism – termed “altermagnetism” – has been building over recent years.
- Now, a SLAC-led team has experimentally proven that a material exhibits characteristics that are theoretically impossible to explain without altermagnetism.
- Altermagnetic materials could be used to design advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Today, in findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism.
“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.”
Building on previous studies, this research confirmed that manganese telluride (MnTe) is an altermagnet – a new class of magnet that exhibits properties of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Their results showed direct experimental evidence of chirality – an asymmetric magnetic structure, akin to a spiral staircase or a screw – in the spins of an altermagnetic candidate material.
Identifying these unique materials could allow researchers to manipulate their properties in ways that make them ideal candidates for advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
A primer on magnetism
To most of us, magnetism is a tangible force: It’s what holds a child's artwork to a refrigerator door and points a compass needle north. But to a physicist, magnetism is more complex. It’s a quantum property of a material, and not all magnetic materials have a directly observable magnetic effect.
In physics, a material is considered magnetic if its electrons’ spins – their internal angular momentum, which can be either “up” or “down” – are polarized, or ordered in a specific pattern.
In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down), creating an observable magnetic field. Humans have known about and made use of this class of magnets since ancient times. In 1933, scientists discovered another type of material with polarized spins. Antiferromagnets have alternating electronic spins (up-down-up-down) that cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect.
A new type of magnetism?
For nearly 90 years, this two-category system dominated our understanding of magnetism.
But in recent years, researchers have noticed that some materials don’t fit neatly into either category. Certain materials seemed to exhibit features of both antiferromagnetism, such as alternating spin configuration with no net magnetization, and ferromagnetism, such as the ability to use spin currents. These behaviors were once thought to be mutually exclusive.
In 2022, researchers proposed the term “altermagnets” to label this wily class of materials.
    
    
We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.
Associate Scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences
To explain this behavior, researchers postulated that altermagnets exhibit an alternating spin polarization (up-down-up-down), much like conventional antiferromagnets, but with a crucial twist: the crystal lattice structure surrounding the “up” spins is rotated relative to the lattice surrounding the “down” spins. This geometric twist is a break in symmetry that could give rise to their unusual behavior.
Chirality: the final piece of the puzzle
“By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real,” Jost said, “but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle.”
That missing piece was experimental evidence of chirality in an altermagnetic candidate material. Chirality, often referred to as “handedness,” means a material cannot be superimposed on a mirror image of itself, just like a left hand cannot fit into a right-handed glove.
Chirality offers a clever way to distinguish subtle, quantum-level differences between antiferromagnets and suspected altermagnets: While an altermagnetic material would have alternating spins (up-down-up-down) like an antiferromagnet, the geometric twists in its lattice would give the material’s electronic and magnetic structure a distinct handedness that conventional antiferromagnets lack.
Jost’s team chose to investigate chirality in MnTe – a material considered antiferromagnetic for decades until a few years ago when it was suspected to be altermagnetic. The team brought it to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France, to a beamline known for its ability to generate highly controlled polarized X-ray beams.
“Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams,” explained Jost. “Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way.”
By scattering circularly polarized X-rays from the material and comparing how it responded to left- versus right-handed light, they teased out a clear chiral signal that shouldn’t exist in a conventional antiferromagnet.
“This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own,” Jost said. The initial experiment was completed in 2024; the team repeated their experiment in early 2025, confirming their earlier results.
“This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties,” said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. “Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible.”
Altermagnetism in the real world
This discovery has big implications for the field of spintronics, where researchers are leveraging the polarized spin of magnetic materials to design next-generation electronics.
Where traditional computing technologies use only an electron’s charge to store and move information, spintronics takes advantage of both an electron’s charge and its spin, giving researchers an additional control knob. Spintronic devices have the potential to be faster, be more robust and significantly decrease power consumption in computing and data centers.
Researchers have had some success with spintronic devices, but that success has been limited by the nature of ferro- and antiferromagnetism.
“Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields,” Jost explained. “If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible – so you can’t easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents.”
“Altermagnets combine the best of both,” Jost said. “They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with.”
Future research will explore how altermagnetic states can be influenced and controlled using light and electricity to enhance their usefulness in spintronic solutions for quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
This research is supported in part by the DOE Office of Science.
Citation: D. Jost et al., Science, 29 October 2026, 10.1126/science.adv3196.
For media inquiries, please contact media@slac.stanford.edu. For other questions or comments, contact SLAC Strategic Communications & External Affairs at communications@slac.stanford.edu.
About SLAC
SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory explores how the universe works at the biggest, smallest and fastest scales and invents powerful tools used by researchers around the globe. As world leaders in ultrafast science and bold explorers of the physics of the universe, we forge new ground in understanding our origins and building a healthier and more sustainable future. Our discovery and innovation help develop new materials and chemical processes and open unprecedented views of the cosmos and life’s most delicate machinery. Building on more than 60 years of visionary research, we help shape the future by advancing areas such as quantum technology, scientific computing and the development of next-generation accelerators.
SLAC is operated by Stanford University for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science. The Office of Science is the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States and is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time.
