articles.title: GUI64 – GUI for the Commodore 64 running on top of the built-in ROM
articles.body:
GUI64
Description[edit | edit source]
GUI64 is a graphical user interface (GUI) for the C64, first released in version 1.0 in November 2024. Although GUI64 may appear to be a standalone operating system, it is just a graphical layer running on top of the C64’s built-in ROM-based operating system, the Kernal. GUI64 presents files and directories in freely movable windows, allowing for easy file management on floppy disks as well as on disk images stored on SD2IEC devices. When GUI64 is running on an Ultimate device, all settings are saved, and disk images can be mounted directly from within the GUI. The current version of GUI64 is 2.0.The current version of GUI64 is 2.1.
Operation[edit | edit source]
GUI64 can be operated using a mouse (such as the 1351 or compatible models) connected to Control Port #1, or with a joystick in Control Port #2 (right click with CBM key + fire). To enable support for the mouse wheel—e.g., for scrolling or in up/down controls (see below)—the Micromys adapter must be used. This functionality is also available when using the VICE emulator.
Look and Feel[edit | edit source]
Starting with version 1.9, GUI64 is available in two variants:
Windows-like interface
In this variant, GUI64 visually resembles Windows-style interfaces. The GUI is window-based, with a taskbar at the bottom of the screen, featuring a "Commodore (CBM) button" embedded on the left and a recessed clock button on the right. In between are the task buttons — similar to those in Windows 95.
Mac-like interface
This variant visually imitates the interface of the first Macintosh computers from Apple. The menus are not integrated into the windows but are displayed in a menu bar at the top edge of the screen. The system menu in the upper-left corner includes, in addition to the entries from the corresponding CBM menu in the Windows variant, an “About” entry, which in the Windows variant is part of the file browser’s menu.
In both versions, the desktop itself is empty except for two drive icons in the upper-left corner (in the Mac design: upper-right corner), and—unlike other interfaces such as C64OS[1] or GEOS—does not support placing file icons directly on it. Instead, the desktop serves as a background for windows, which can be freely moved and positioned. Unlike GEOS, for example, GUI64 does not use the VIC-II’s bitmap graphics mode, but operates in text mode. GUI64 is therefore character set–based. For instance, windows cannot be moved pixel-perfectly, but are instead aligned to the 8×8-pixel grid of the character screen. The desktop consists of 22 rows (in the Mac design: 24 rows) and 40 columns of characters. Strictly speaking, GUI64 should therefore be considered not a GUI, but a TUI (Text User Interface).
Elements on the Desktop and in the Taskbar[edit | edit source]
Drive Icons[edit | edit source]
By default, the two drive icons are assigned to device numbers 8 and 9, but this can be changed via right-click on the icons or, alternatively, in the menu of the associated browser window. A double-click on a drive icon opens a file browser window, see below.
Ultimate Icon[edit | edit source]
If an Ultimate cartridge is connected to the C64, or if the computer itself is an Ultimate device, and if the Ultimate Command Interface is enabled, a third desktop icon in the shape of a USB flash drive has been available since version 1.98: the Ultimate icon. Double-clicking this icon opens a browser window that provides access to the file system of a USB flash drive (or SD card) connected to the Ultimate device, allowing disk images to be mounted directly from within GUI64.
[edit | edit source]
Clicking the Commodore button in the lower-left corner of the taskbar opens a menu with three entries: "Settings", "About", and "BASIC". Starting with version 1.98, Ultimate owners will also see an additional "Reboot" entry, which reboots the C64. Selecting "BASIC" (after confirming the prompt) launches the familiar C64 BASIC editor. Clicking "Settings" opens a configuration window where the appearance of GUI64 can be customized. If GUI64 detects an Ultimate system with the Command Interface enabled, the settings are stored in the Ultimate's flash folder as of version 1.97. These settings include various color options as well as an option to display the desktop with a dotted background. Clicking "About" opens a dialog containing information about GUI64.
Time[edit | edit source]
Since version 1.96, the clock automatically displays the Ultimate's time (provided an Ultimate cartridge is connected or the C64 is FPGA-based on an Ultimate 64 board and the Ultimate Command Interface is enabled). Since version 2.0, the clock also displays the correct time when a WiC64 module is connected to the user port. Double-clicking the clock opens a dialog box for adjusting the time. If no Ultimate system or WiC64 is detected when GUI64 starts, the time is set to “00:00” by default.
Tooltips[edit | edit source]
Because the GUI64 screen has limited horizontal space, taskbar button titles are truncated to fit. Starting with GUI64 v1.8.1, users can see the full title in a tooltip by hovering over a button for at least one second. Tooltips are also displayed when hovering over desktop drive icons, showing the full path for drives such as SD2IEC or the Ultimate.
Graphical Elements on the Desktop[edit | edit source]
Windows[edit | edit source]
The primary graphical elements that convey information in GUI64 are windows. Each window has a title bar at the top, with the window title on the left (Mac design: centered). In the Windows design, there are various control buttons on the right. One of these buttons is always an X-icon (X) to close the window; if the window supports minimizing or maximizing, corresponding buttons for those actions are also present. In the Mac version, there is only a button for closing the window on the left-hand side of the title bar. Windows-version: A minimized window disappears from the desktop but remains accessible as a button in the taskbar. Clicking this button restores the window to the desktop. This helps keep the desktop organized and clutter-free.
A special type of window is the dialog. Dialogs cannot be minimized and always retain full focus. This means that user input is restricted to within the dialog window only.
Controls[edit | edit source]
The graphical elements within windows are called controls. Each of these controls serves a specific function—even if that function is simply displaying text, as is the case with labels (see below). The controls available in the current version of GUI64 are, in order:
Functionality[edit | edit source]
GUI64 allows users to work with drives and files. The following drives are detected and supported: Commodore 1541 floppy drive, Commodore 1571 floppy drive, Commodore 1581 floppy drive, and SD2IEC devices. GUI64 may also work with hard drives and other storage devices; however, due to a lack of testing, reliable functionality for these cannot be guaranteed at this time.
Double-clicking one of the drive icons on the desktop opens a file browser window, which—after loading—displays the contents of the medium (floppy disk, SD2IEC directory, or disk image within an SD2IEC directory). GUI64 can also handle dnp images. Files and directories are listed vertically within the window. Each entry shows the file type (as an icon), the file name, and, optionally, the file size (see the "View Menu" below). Entries can be selected by clicking on them. The list can be scrolled by either using the scrollbar on the right edge or the mouse wheel.
Running Programs[edit | edit source]
To run programs (equivalent to LOAD"...",x and RUN), a simple double-click on the corresponding entry in the drive window is required. This will display a progress bar in a seperate window, showing the loading progress. Once the file is loaded into the C64's memory, the file will be executed. To load a machine code file (without a BASIC stub, such as 10 SYS 2063), see "Boot" in the File menu. Note: GUI64 will not remain in the background after running a file and has to be loaded back into memory afterwards, e.g. by pressing the Reset button if GUI64 was loaded from cartridge.
Opening Directories and Disk Images on SD2IEC Drives[edit | edit source]
When the file browser window displays the contents of a directory on an SD2IEC drive, directories and disk images (if available) will also be shown. Directories are represented by a folder-like icon. A double-click on a directory or disk image initiates a loading process, after which the contents of the selected directory or disk image will be displayed in the browser window.
Menus[edit | edit source]
Each file browser window in GUI64 has a menu consisting of the entries "Disk," "File," and "View." These menus provide the user with various options for manipulating drives, files, and directories.
The Disk Menu[edit | edit source]
The 'Disk' menu in GUI64 allows users to manipulate floppy disks (or disk images) and view information about the drive at the corresponding device number.
The File Menu[edit | edit source]
The 'File' menu of GUI64 allows for copying or 'cutting' files, as well as deleting, renaming, viewing, booting files, and creating disk images.
*Note: After creating a new image, the corresponding virtual disk needs to be formatted. For this, double click the image, click Format in the Disk menu and choose Full Format.
The View Menu[edit | edit source]
With the entries in the 'View' menu, the display in the file browser window can be changed.
Applications[edit | edit source]
Currently, there are no applications for GUI64. However, after the release of version 2.0, an interface for developers is planned, which will allow for the easy creation of applications for GUI64.
Development[edit | edit source]
GUI64 was developed by Friedrich (Fritz) Philipp, also known as WebFritzi. Especially during the implementation of the drive functions, he received valuable support from numerous members of Forum64, who assisted him with advice and guidance. Some code snippets originate from Codebase64.

articles.title: V100 SXM2 pinout and NVLink reference
articles.body:
This project aims to become an open-source carrier-board design for NVIDIA V100 SXM2 modules, including NVLink connections for two- and four-GPU configurations.
While that board is being developed, this reference kit shares the pin mappings, connection plans and connector-only KiCad resources so other people can develop their own designs.
My contribution so far is primarily curation: gathering public information, comparing sources, reconciling connector orientation and signal names, and making the results easier to follow. The original reverse-engineering work belongs to its authors, credited in Sources and attribution.
- Download the complete reference ZIP from v0.1.0-reference, or use Code > Download ZIP for the current development files.
- Extract the archive and keep the directory structure. Choose a single-, two- or four-module KiCad starter, then open its .kicad_pro file in KiCad 10.0.7 or a compatible newer version. Keep the whole kicad/ folder so the shared symbol library is available.
- For reading without KiCad, use the complete schematic PDFs or standalone workbook.
The download guide includes print editions and library-path help. Change notes identify reference editions. This is a public reference pre-release, not a hardware-qualified carrier board.
- 800 canonical contacts: 400 on connector A and 400 on connector B, with signal names, evidence and electrical-treatment notes.
- Two- and four-GPU connection tables: exact Connector B pads, directions, lanes and polarity.
- Three editable KiCad starters: one module’s A/B connectors, plus two- and four-module versions with NVLink data connected. Every contact stays labelled, including unconnected clocks, power and control pins. No regulator, power-control or clock circuits are included.
- Catppuccin Mocha visuals: contact maps, topology diagrams, schematic previews and the standalone dark reference workbook. An optional KiCad colour theme is included.
External clock required: the NVLink starter schematics show data wiring, not a complete working NVLink implementation. Each V100 needs a 156.25 MHz differential NVHS clock on B/E20 (+) and B/F20 (−). The separate PCIe clock is 100 MHz on A/E7 (+) and A/F7 (−). Clock requirements and scope.
Presence detection and simple carriers: the full reference-carrier presence loop is not established as a universal requirement for basic GPU operation. Reported simple carriers omit the feature, while a controller that waits for a presence signal needs that signal handled correctly. See basic operation versus presence-detection features, including the two connector-A contacts whose ground labels are under review. This distinction does not make other supporting circuitry optional.
These are the actual connector-only KiCad schematics: 400 labelled contacts on A and 400 on B. Click a preview to open the full-size vector drawing. The two- and four-GPU NVLink arrangements are shown separately below and in the connection guides.
Open the KiCad project · Schematic overview · KiCad guide
The full six-group two-GPU arrangement is derived from the documented pairing families; the four-GPU arrangement follows the curated topology. Each guide explains its source evidence and remaining uncertainties. These are logical connection plans, not routed bridge schematics.
Open the two-V100 KiCad project · Native schematic previews
Open the four-V100 KiCad project · Native schematic previews
Two-GPU connections · Four-GPU connections
The actual local reference footprint, exported directly by KiCad: 800 contact pads, housing outlines and mounting features. A raw PCB footprint is not included in this edition; see footprint availability and open questions and visual provenance.
This is a render of an existing project geometry preview, using the Amphenol connector model. It illustrates connector placement; it is not a completed carrier board or proof of connector A/B identity, mating-part selection or viewing direction. See render provenance.
The longer-term goal is a reusable open-source board design. This reference kit currently covers the pin mappings, NVLink connection plans and connector starter. Routed boards, manufacturing outputs and hardware qualification are future work. See the roadmap.
Corrections are particularly useful when they include an oriented drawing, exact source reference, continuity result or measured behaviour. Please distinguish a confirmed observation from an interpretation.
Use the correction and file-help forms, following the contribution guide. To reference this edition in your own work, use GitHub's Cite this repository option or CITATION.cff, and retain the relevant upstream source credits.
Our original hardware design contributions use CERN-OHL-W-2.0; our original documentation, diagrams and workbook presentation use CC BY-SA 4.0. Both allow commercial reuse, with attribution/notices and the applicable reciprocal sharing requirements. See licence scope and full texts and third-party notices. The licences do not claim ownership of pinout facts or replace upstream terms.
Follow the project and join the discussion on the Level1Techs forums: designing an open-source budget 4× V100 SXM2 NVLink backplane.
Thank you to everyone on the Level1Techs forums for your help, ideas and contributions to this project.

articles.title: Apple reports fourth quarter results
articles.body:
PRESS RELEASE
                    
                    
                        November 2, 2026
                    
                    
                
Apple reports fourth quarter results
                
                
                    September quarter records for total company revenue, iPhone revenue, and EPS 
Services revenue reaches new all-time high
                
            
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced financial results for its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter ended September 26, 2026. The Company posted quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year over year. Company gross margin was 47.9 percent, including a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point from tariff refunds. articles.title: Ballot Rejections Have Soared in Rural Counties as USPS Reduces Mail Service
articles.body:
Reporting Highlights
- Rural Cuts: Delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, a ProPublica analysis found.
- Rejected Ballots: The rates of ballots rejected for arriving late this year doubled or tripled in areas affected by the cuts compared to the 2022 primary. That wasn’t the case elsewhere.
- Extraordinary Measures: Postal Service leaders say special procedures in place for the Nov. 3 election should prevent similar delays, but experts warn that mistakes are likely.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.
Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.
Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.
In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.
But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.
Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.
The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.
In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.
Help Us Report on Key Election Issues
ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?
In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.
Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.
Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.
“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”
Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.
At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.
“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”
Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.
“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'”
A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)
After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.
At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.
Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.
“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”
Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.
The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.
When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)
The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.
Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.
The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.
Mail Services Have Been Cut in 16,000 More ZIP Codes Since the 2024 Election
A pilot program that reduced mail pickups to save money was paused in the lead-up to the 2024 election. The rollout has since resumed, and the changes have been made in five times as many ZIP codes for the 2026 midterms.
In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.
This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.
Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.
A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.
“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,'” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”
Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.
Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.
In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.
In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.
Has Mail Service Been Reduced in Your ZIP Code?
If the frequency of mail pickups has been reduced in your area, mail may take longer to send and receive, and the date on the postmark could be later than the day you dropped it off, which may matter for mail like ballots that is subject to a deadline.
In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.
“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”
In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.
Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.
Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.
Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.
Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.
The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.
ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)
Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.
“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.
Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.
A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.
In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.
Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.
In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.
“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.
“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.
If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.
Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.
For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses  and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .
We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.
In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.
In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.
In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:
We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.
In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.
We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.
For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.
It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.
Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.
We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.
Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.
Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.
            We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.
        
We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.
            The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along (Figure 1). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python.
        
Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.
So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.
            We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment . To do so, it needs to reverse the car for some distance, such that it has enough runway to accelerate long enough to overcome the ramp. However, the PPO network converges to a local-minimum policy where it drives straight at the ramp and gets stuck.
We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.
From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.
Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.
            We take three MinAtar games : Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. For each of them, we provide Astra the game rules and source code, and the corresponding network. There is no access to data, loss, gradients, and tools. We also do not allow Astra to roll out the network in the environment. With just the network weights and environment description, Astra generates the new weights in text directly, after which we evaluate the new network.
        
Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.
How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.
So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.
From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.
We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.
Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.
We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.
With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins more than half of its games against two smaller PPO networks (243 → 32 → 32 → 82). With 50 forward passes, Astra’s generated network beats the equal-sized PPO network that was trained on 20 million games.
How does it do it: Astra writes the network as a small Go program, layer by layer, in Python. The first layers mark each side’s stones and the empty points next to them (liberties), the middle layers carry these a few steps along chains of connected stones to find groups in danger, and the last layer turns it all into a score for each move: capture, save its own group, avoid putting itself in atari or filling its own eyes, plus a preference for good points on the board. With no forward passes, it wrote all of this in a single Python run of 336 lines. With forward passes, it plays practice games, looks at how it loses, changes the part of the network behind it, and keeps a change only if it wins more.
Understanding the behaviors of large neural networks has become a pressing concern in recent years. Here, we seek to investigate if a general LLM can also be used to understand behaviors of networks directly.
            We fine-tune two copies of Gemma 3 270M in exactly the same way, on the same QA datasetThe QA dataset: GitHub.. One copy is trained to give the correct answer. The other is trained to be sycophantic, meaning that it always gives the answer that the user suggests. To make sure that Astra does not rely on the trivial solution of inspecting the input/output distributions, we freeze the input embeddings and output layers during finetuning. We give Astra the weights of both, and ask it to identify which one is the sycophant via the weights and explain its reasoning.
        
Unfortunately, from the weights alone, Astra was unable to tell. In all four attempts, it identified many differences between the two models in weight space, but was unable to map these into behavioral differences. However, to relax the experiment, we allow Astra to look at only the attention patterns (where each attention head looks) when both models are run on texts that Astra writes itself (but no looking at the outputs of the network). Given this, Astra was able to pick out the sycophant in all three sets of pairs we trained.
It was also able to reason about how they differ. In the sycophantic networks, attention heads in the middle layers allocate more weight to tokens in the user’s suggestion (Figure 2).
Finally, we scale up to a larger language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, and ask Astra to improve its math reasoning capabilities by editing the weights.
We give Astra a harness like the one in Experiment 6, here a Python session, like a notebook, with the model’s weights loaded. Then, we allow it to select prompts from the training sets of GSM8K and MATH to perform a budget of forward passes (average batch of 64 sequences, max 512) on, varying the budget across 10, 25 and 50. Again, no training or gradient information is allowed.
            As a result, Astra spots and fixes a common failure of tiny reasoning models: they loop . When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.
        
With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.
Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.
Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.
Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.
            Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .
        
            On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.
        
In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.
This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:
We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.
We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number. The edited Qwen3.5-0.8B from Experiment 8 is on Hugging Face. We thank Ahsen Khaliq at Hugging Face for rebuilding it from these logs, re-running its evaluation, and making a live demo.
Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!
Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.
Please cite this post as
Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights.” November 2026. https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/
or in BibTeX

  author       = {Takehi, Rikiya and Teoh, Jayden and Zhang, Alex and Khattab, Omar},

  month        = nov,

When the base model loops, it repeats the same text and rarely reaches an answer (85 of its first 96 practice answers ran to the 32,768-token limit). Astra traced the looping to one direction written by the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted that direction from 64 output columns in each (131,072 weights), much like removing a behavior by deleting a single direction from a model’s weights.
        
With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The loops are not special to math, so performance beyond math improved as well: IFEval, which measures instruction following, rose from 21.0% to 62.3%. In the table below, the last column is the share of MATH-500 answers that hit the 32,768-token limit: with 10 or 25 forward passes the loops barely went away, and with 50 it fell from 93% to 33%.
Importantly, the edit changes only 131,072 of the model’s 0.8 billion weights (0.016%). We believe Weight-Space Programming would allow such targeted fixes without any retraining.
Fixing loops, however, is not the same as making a model better at math: it lets the model finish answers it could already work out. So we also tried Gemma 3 270M, an instruction-tuned model about a third the size of Qwen3.5-0.8B, which rarely loops: only 8.5% of its answers reach its token limit, against 93% for Qwen. Here, Astra could not improve it. Reading Gemma’s failures, Astra found ordinary reasoning errors, such as wrong arithmetic and invalid algebraic steps, with no single component behind them to switch off. Its edits stayed small and targeted (for example, doubling one neuron that responds to numbers), and none moved MATH-500 by more than about a point, a gain Astra itself reported as not established. Editing weights could remove an obstacle that hid an ability, but it could not add an ability the model lacked. Gemma was sampled with its model card’s setting (temperature 1.0, top-k 64, top-p 0.95, up to 8,192 tokens), and its MATH-500 scores average 4 samples per problem.
Neural networks are hard for us to read, and hard to work with directly.
            Mechanistic interpretability reads networks with tools built for the job, tracing circuits and features and editing weights . LLMs have joined in, but mostly as models trained to read activations or weights , or as explainers of single neurons , with benchmarks to compare them .
        
            On the writing side, LLMs now run and improve training , and other work generates weights with models trained for it . Gradient-free methods still find weights by trial and error . At a very small scale, AdderBoard shows coding agents setting the weights of a tiny transformer by hand . Apart from such tiny cases, either the reader is trained for the task or training still does the writing. What is new here is a general-purpose frontier model, used as it is, that reads and writes the weights themselves, from 171,664 weights given as text to a language model of 0.8 billion weights with tools.
        
In this blog, we demonstrated the rising capability of LLMs to read and write neural network weights (i.e., the rising concept of Weight-Space Programming). Our current results do show that capabilities are exciting but still limited, specifically due to inefficiencies in context length and harnesses. However, the current signs do show strong potential for a future involving Weight-Space Programming. We believe this marks the beginning of a dramatic shift in fields like mechanistic interpretability and neural network optimization.
This opens up radical new possibilities for LLMs to function as a translator between human language and the weight space. Here are some examples:
We are currently building a benchmark and a harness for LLMs’ capability on Weight-Space Programming. We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline.
We release the complete logs of every experiment in this post at github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. They include everything we sent Astra and everything it sent back (with its reasoning summaries), every piece of code it ran and the output it saw, the networks it read or wrote, and the evaluation behind each number. The edited Qwen3.5-0.8B from Experiment 8 is on Hugging Face. We thank Ahsen Khaliq at Hugging Face for rebuilding it from these logs, re-running its evaluation, and making a live demo.
Rikiya thanks Jacob Li and Akihisa Watanabe for valuable discussions on the very first iterations of this research, about LLMs' potential capability to write neural network weights. Rikiya also thanks Souradip Chakraborty, Matei Zaharia and his students in Berkeley Sky Lab, Heather Miller and her students at CMU, and researchers in cmpnd for the fruitful discussions on the earlier iterations!
Jayden thanks Zico Kolter for early discussions on LLMs being able to write neural network weights zero-shot, which also shaped the direction of this project.
Please cite this post as
Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights.” November 2026. https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/
or in BibTeX
@misc{takehi2026weightspace,
  title        = {{Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read \& write neural network weights}},
  author       = {Takehi, Rikiya and Teoh, Jayden and Zhang, Alex and Khattab, Omar},
  year         = {2026},
  month        = nov,
  howpublished = {\url{https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/}},
  note         = {Blog post}
}

articles.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
articles.body:
New-device 2FA prompt skipped
At a consumer fintech app, a login routing change bypassed the new-device verification step.
A security checkpoint was silently skipped.
Mo is an AI QA engineer that tests your app end to end. Verify critical flows and find bugs from a prompt.
Trusted by leading engineering teams.
Trusted in production by teams shipping every day.
Code moves faster. Verification has to keep up.
Coding agents have made it dramatically faster to build software. The bottleneck is now knowing it works. Verification belongs in the agent loop. Agents need evidence from the app itself to verify that their changes deliver the intended behavior.
Explore
Write the user flows you need to verify. Momentic runs the tests against your app. Reuse successful AI actions and review proposed repairs as the app changes.
1 of 5
Verification from your editor to CI.
 Write steps and assertions in plain-English YAML.
Review and version the tests in your repository. 
Describe a user flow and its expected result in plain English. Keep the steps and assertions in YAML files your team and coding agent can review.
fileType: momentic/test/v2id: standard-user-checkouturl: https://shop.momentic.aidescription: End-to-end checkout flowsteps:  - module: ./log-in-username-password.module.yaml  - act: add the momentic backpack to the cart and go to checkout  - module: ./fill-out-personal-info.module.yaml  - assert: the item total matches the amount listed for each item  - click: Finish button
Use the CLI to check the app you're changing. Run the same tests in CI before the next merge or deploy.
See which step failed and inspect its screenshots and traces. AI triage investigates the cause and proposes a test repair for you to review.
  - click: Place Order button
Momentic finds controls again when the UI changes. Permanent healing proposes test-file edits for review. Apply the diff and rerun to check the result.
Describe your product’s terminology, business rules, and expected behavior in the Knowledge base. Agents use that context to choose actions and check outcomes.
Give agents the product rules they need to check a flow.
Maps screens and user flows seen during test runs.
Review session suggestions before adding them to the Knowledge base.
Loved by engineering teams.
“Momentic gave us a fast and reliable way to validate Poe.com's AI responses, even when they weren't deterministic.”
30 min
daily test execution, down from 7 hours
500+
manual test cases replaced
100%
critical tests created in one month
Test private apps with SSO and custom data policies. Get dedicated onboarding and priority support. Momentic is SOC 2 Type 2 certified.
Engineering teams using Momentic.
Independently audited. Compliance reports in the Trust Center.
Service scope and uptime commitments are set in your Enterprise agreement.
SAML and OIDC SSO, Admin and Member roles, and audit logs.
Priority support and a dedicated account manager for enterprise accounts.
Examples of application failures found by Momentic, with the affected flow and its impact.
Mo is out of beta. Start a session from your coding agent, the app, a PR comment, or the qa CLI. A separate agent reproduces each functional bug before Mo reports it.
We graded Mo, Codex, Claude Code, and Devin on 20 areas of Gitea, Metabase, Twenty, and Saleor. With 60 minutes per area, Mo found about 269 labeled bugs. The next best agent found about 86.
Start Mo from a PR comment, a label, or the CLI. It tests the PR's preview deployment, posts a review with its findings, and sets a Mo commit check.
Pick low, medium, high, or max for each session, from about 15 minutes of testing for a pull request to about 2 hours for a whole app.
Accept, dismiss, fix, or reopen a bug with qa bugs. A retest keeps the finding and its history, and marks it fixed when Mo can no longer reproduce it.
Run your tests on browsers Momentic manages. The knowledge base is generally available too, and classification, triage, and AI test selection dropped their beta labels.
Mo runs autonomous QA sessions in the cloud, on web or hosted Android and iOS devices, with your org's MCP servers and secrets attached to the session.
Each v5 locator and assertion query now routes itself to a fast, medium, or extended effort based on how much reasoning it needs, which also sets its credit usage.
Generated ids are normalized and source-file attributes are left out of the cached selector, so rebuilding your app no longer misses every step.
An AI action can cache a branch now, so the cookie banner that only shows up half the time replays from cache instead of waking the agent again.
A separate reviewer looks at where the app actually ended up before an AI action passes, and hands the step back with its reasoning when your goal did not happen.
Triage works out what broke each test. It commits the fixes your branch caused, then opens a pull request for every other cause and asks whoever owns it to review.
Run Android tests on hosted emulators without Android Studio, the SDK, or adb installed on your machine.
Say in plain English what should have been true at some point in a run. Momentic checks it against frames from the run video, so a toast that flashes for a second still counts.
Commit what your agents keep getting wrong about your app to .momentic/skills, and the explore, triage, and result-classification agents read it while they run.
momentic doctor tells you what is wrong with your setup: CLI and Node versions, sign-in, browsers, project config, and the connection to Momentic. --fix clears out deprecated options.
Pull your finished runs and run groups over REST with an API key. Page through them by cursor and filter by date, status, or platform.
Capture resolved tests into portable snapshots and replay them in isolation with momentic run --from-snapshot.
momentic ai explore now supports deeper planning controls, JSON output, and product bug reports with repro steps.
Runs now expose live progress, structured JSON output, and clearer Run Viewer diagnostics for cache status, retries, conditionals, and loops.
The V3 agent is now the default everywhere. It plans the flow up front, caches the resolved steps, and self-heals on failure.
momentic ai triage groups failures into labeled buckets, previews the plan with a dry run, and can quarantine what it cannot fix.
New projects scaffold in the cleaner v2 file format, and momentic upgrade migrates existing projects end to end.
Pass --parallel auto and Momentic sizes the worker pool from your host's CPU count for faster local and CI runs.
Provision ephemeral inboxes with email.create() and lease numbers from your org pool with sms.lease() right inside a test.
The recovery flow can inspect browser state, run steps, retry the failed step, and refresh stale caches, with per-step visibility.
momentic ai classify categorizes a run from its ID or URL so you can route each failure category to the right action.
Android AI actions now plan up front, cache resolved steps, and self-heal, matching the web experience.
Screen recordings are captured automatically during iOS and Android test runs and stored with the run attempt.
Create tests and modules, run step ranges, and drive emulator sessions for iOS and Android from Claude Code or Cursor.
AI actions are enabled by default, so the ai.aiAction switch is no longer needed in momentic.config.yaml.
Mobile tests gain dedicated setup and teardown sections so shared preconditions and cleanup live in one place.
Author and run Momentic tests against iOS, with modules, AI actions, and hosted simulators alongside Android.
Start and terminate browser sessions, splice steps, and run step ranges from your coding agent over a stdio MCP server.
New request listener, request recording, and mock route step types let agents capture and stub network traffic.
The Run Viewer now charts system and process CPU and memory captured during execution to help debug flaky runs.
Failure recovery now extends to mobile tests, retrying and adapting around transient issues on iOS and Android.
momentic results view launches a local run viewer to browse results on your machine without uploading anything.
Step back and forward through edits in the mobile editor while authoring tests.

articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
articles.body:
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.
It enables developers to:
- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.
To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository.
Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the
Apache License 2.0. Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. This project
is currently not accepting external contributions.
- Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
- Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
- Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth.
- Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
- Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack.
Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
NVIDIA API catalog (integrate.api.nvidia.com) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:
- LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
- Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
- Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2
The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT, DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL,
EMBED_ENDPOINT, and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables —
<PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY, and <PREFIX>_MODEL:
You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>. So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL, NON_REASONING_MODEL). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.
- Docker with Docker Compose v2 (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows,
Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see
DEPLOYMENT.md.
- An NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from
the NVIDIA API catalog at https://build.nvidia.com.
- Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query (Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB).
Kubernetes
To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see DEPLOYMENT.md.
Local (Docker Compose)
- Clone the repository: git clone <repo-url> auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology
- Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values
(Postgres credentials, DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY, CONNECTION_STRINGS, etc.).
See .env.example for the full list of variables:
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env Note: 
  - AUTH_SECRET and APP_URL are required — without them every page
fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error.
  - POSTGRES_PORT only changes the host-side port mapping (set it if
5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres
on the internal network port.
- Build the images and start the stack: docker compose up -d --build This builds the backend (auto_ontology) and frontend (auto-ontology-frontend) images, brings
up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot frontend-migrate job to
sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service,
and frontend).
- Open the UI at http://localhost:3000 (the backend API is on :3001,
pgAdmin on :5050).
Troubleshooting: if the UI loads without the left navigation panel
(or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a
stale session cookie — this happens when AUTH_SECRET changes or the
database is reset. Clear the site data for localhost:3000 (or delete
the better-auth.session_token cookie) and sign in again.
Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources:
- Added through the UI — connections created from within the app. With this option the connection credentials are stored in plaintext in Postgres unless Vault is configured: 
  - Without Vault: the full connection object (including the password) is JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row.
  - With Vault: the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the lookup key — there is no separate reference field).
Vault is enabled only when all of VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_NAMESPACE, VAULT_ROLE_ID, and VAULT_SECRET_ID are set (VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT and VAULT_KV_MOUNT are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial
configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage.
- CONNECTION_STRINGS environment variable — a comma-separated list of
connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm --set connectionStrings=<CONNECTION-STRINGS> flag). This is a fallback: it
is used only when there are no UI-added connections.
Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication. The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback
A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an API token instead:
- Open the user menu (top right) → API Tokens → New token.
- Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and copy the token. Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it means minting a new one.
Send it as x-api-key on any /api/... call — Authorization: Bearer <token>
works too:
curl -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/termsimport os
import requests
session = requests.Session()
session.headers["x-api-key"] = os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]
terms = session.get("https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms").json()
answer = session.post(
    "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions",
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
).json()
Things worth knowing:
- A token acts as its owner. It carries no permissions of its own — every call is authorized against the owner's role, exactly as it would be in the browser. A viewer's token cannot do admin things.
- The whole API surface accepts it. Authentication is resolved in one place
(frontend/auth/resolve-user.ts) for every route, so any endpoint in docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json that is not withPublic works with a token.
- Revocation is immediate. Delete the token in the UI, or delete/ban the owning user, and the next request with it gets a 401.
- Tokens cannot manage tokens. Creating and revoking requires a signed-in session, so a leaked token cannot issue itself successors.
Public clients call the authenticated Next.js gateway at
POST /api/chat/completions. The response is an SSE stream containing step,
result, or error events, followed by [DONE].
conversation_id is optional:
- Omit it for a stateless, one-shot request.
- Supply a client-generated UUID to create or continue a conversation.
- Reuse the same UUID for every turn in the thread. Wait for [DONE] before
sending the next turn; overlapping requests for one conversation return 409 Conversation in progress.
{
  "question": "What about last month?",
  "conversation_id": "d61d8aa3-d496-4fa7-97ce-4f831c162e7f"
}
For conversational requests, FastAPI loads up to the five most recent completed turns (bounded to 12,000 characters) and rewrites contextual input such as “What about August?” into a standalone question before running the existing text-to-SQL graph. Independent questions are passed through unchanged. Internal agent thoughts, chart payloads, errors, and raw SQL result sets are not reused as context.
Conversation history is scoped to the authenticated Auto Ontology user. Browser and
service callers should use the Next.js gateway, which resolves the user and
forwards the internal x-auto-ontology-user-id header to FastAPI. The FastAPI port is a
trusted internal service boundary: it must not be exposed publicly because that
header is not independently verified by FastAPI. A direct FastAPI request
without conversation_id remains stateless; a direct request with
conversation_id requires the trusted identity header.
The web UI manages the UUID automatically. An API-created conversation can be
opened in the UI at /chat?focus=<conversation_id> when it belongs to the
signed-in user.
Coding agents: start at AGENTS.md. Skills live in
skills/ (nvidia-ontology-setup, nvidia-ontology-management, nvidia-ontology-query).
Maintainers keep using CLAUDE.md.
Agent harnesses such as Cursor and Claude Desktop can query your data through
Auto Ontology's MCP server. See
mcp/ to run it and docs/mcp.md for the details.
Auto Ontology is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
SPDX identifier: Apache-2.0.
Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form:
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2024-2026, NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES.
All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
Third-party open-source components used by Auto Ontology are enumerated, with their
