articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
articles.body:
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.
It enables developers to:
- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.
To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository.
Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the
Apache License 2.0. Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. This project
is currently not accepting external contributions.
- Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
- Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
- Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth.
- Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
- Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack.
Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
NVIDIA API catalog (integrate.api.nvidia.com) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:
- LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
- Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
- Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2
The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT, DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL,
EMBED_ENDPOINT, and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables —
<PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY, and <PREFIX>_MODEL:
You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>. So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL, NON_REASONING_MODEL). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.
- Docker with Docker Compose v2 (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows,
Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see
DEPLOYMENT.md.
- An NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from
the NVIDIA API catalog at https://build.nvidia.com.
- Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query (Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB).
Kubernetes
To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see DEPLOYMENT.md.
Local (Docker Compose)
- Clone the repository: git clone <repo-url> auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology
- Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values
(Postgres credentials, DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY, CONNECTION_STRINGS, etc.).
See .env.example for the full list of variables:
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env Note: 
  - AUTH_SECRET and APP_URL are required — without them every page
fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error.
  - POSTGRES_PORT only changes the host-side port mapping (set it if
5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres
on the internal network port.
- Build the images and start the stack: docker compose up -d --build This builds the backend (auto_ontology) and frontend (auto-ontology-frontend) images, brings
up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot frontend-migrate job to
sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service,
and frontend).
- Open the UI at http://localhost:3000 (the backend API is on :3001,
pgAdmin on :5050).
Troubleshooting: if the UI loads without the left navigation panel
(or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a
stale session cookie — this happens when AUTH_SECRET changes or the
database is reset. Clear the site data for localhost:3000 (or delete
the better-auth.session_token cookie) and sign in again.
Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources:
- Added through the UI — connections created from within the app. With this option the connection credentials are stored in plaintext in Postgres unless Vault is configured: 
  - Without Vault: the full connection object (including the password) is JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row.
  - With Vault: the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the lookup key — there is no separate reference field).
Vault is enabled only when all of VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_NAMESPACE, VAULT_ROLE_ID, and VAULT_SECRET_ID are set (VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT and VAULT_KV_MOUNT are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial
configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage.
- CONNECTION_STRINGS environment variable — a comma-separated list of
connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm --set connectionStrings=<CONNECTION-STRINGS> flag). This is a fallback: it
is used only when there are no UI-added connections.
Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication. The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback
A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an API token instead:
- Open the user menu (top right) → API Tokens → New token.
- Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and copy the token. Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it means minting a new one.
Send it as x-api-key on any /api/... call — Authorization: Bearer <token>
works too:
curl -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/termsimport os
import requests
session = requests.Session()
session.headers["x-api-key"] = os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]
terms = session.get("https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms").json()
answer = session.post(
    "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions",
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
).json()
Things worth knowing:
- A token acts as its owner. It carries no permissions of its own — every call is authorized against the owner's role, exactly as it would be in the browser. A viewer's token cannot do admin things.
- The whole API surface accepts it. Authentication is resolved in one place
(frontend/auth/resolve-user.ts) for every route, so any endpoint in docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json that is not withPublic works with a token.
- Revocation is immediate. Delete the token in the UI, or delete/ban the owning user, and the next request with it gets a 401.
- Tokens cannot manage tokens. Creating and revoking requires a signed-in session, so a leaked token cannot issue itself successors.
Public clients call the authenticated Next.js gateway at
POST /api/chat/completions. The response is an SSE stream containing step,
result, or error events, followed by [DONE].
conversation_id is optional:
- Omit it for a stateless, one-shot request.
- Supply a client-generated UUID to create or continue a conversation.
- Reuse the same UUID for every turn in the thread. Wait for [DONE] before
sending the next turn; overlapping requests for one conversation return 409 Conversation in progress.
{
  "question": "What about last month?",
  "conversation_id": "d61d8aa3-d496-4fa7-97ce-4f831c162e7f"
}
For conversational requests, FastAPI loads up to the five most recent completed turns (bounded to 12,000 characters) and rewrites contextual input such as “What about August?” into a standalone question before running the existing text-to-SQL graph. Independent questions are passed through unchanged. Internal agent thoughts, chart payloads, errors, and raw SQL result sets are not reused as context.
Conversation history is scoped to the authenticated Auto Ontology user. Browser and
service callers should use the Next.js gateway, which resolves the user and
forwards the internal x-auto-ontology-user-id header to FastAPI. The FastAPI port is a
trusted internal service boundary: it must not be exposed publicly because that
header is not independently verified by FastAPI. A direct FastAPI request
without conversation_id remains stateless; a direct request with
conversation_id requires the trusted identity header.
The web UI manages the UUID automatically. An API-created conversation can be
opened in the UI at /chat?focus=<conversation_id> when it belongs to the
signed-in user.
Coding agents: start at AGENTS.md. Skills live in
skills/ (nvidia-ontology-setup, nvidia-ontology-management, nvidia-ontology-query).
Maintainers keep using CLAUDE.md.
Agent harnesses such as Cursor and Claude Desktop can query your data through
Auto Ontology's MCP server. See
mcp/ to run it and docs/mcp.md for the details.
Auto Ontology is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
SPDX identifier: Apache-2.0.
Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form:
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2024-2026, NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES.
All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

upstream licenses and project URLs, in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Components added by the
container images are listed separately in
CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

articles.title: Vibe-Coding a Game in 2026: What AI Builds, What Breaks
articles.body:
Key takeaways
- In late October 2026 a well-known developer wrote that building games that play well is "shockingly easy now", and Roblox told shareholders that people had published over 70,000 games with its prompt-to-game tool.
- AI is strong at the first playable version: small browser games in three.js or Phaser, placeholder art and even code-generated music.
- It is still weak at the parts players and brands pay for: game logic that holds up over a long session, consistent art and animation, multiplayer, cheat-proof leaderboards, payments and performance on ordinary phones.
- Platform rules apply to AI games: Steam asks for an AI disclosure, Google Play requires in-app reporting for AI-generated content, and Apple rejects copycats and spam.
- A prototype you made yourself is a strong brief for a studio. Once a game carries prizes, personal data or payments, it needs engineering and testing.
The short answer: yes, in 2026 you can vibe-code a small, playable game in an evening by describing it to an AI model, and a prototype like that is now a perfectly sensible first step. What you can't skip is the work between "playable on my phone" and "live in front of customers": fixing logic bugs that only appear in long sessions, making the art consistent, testing on mid-range Android phones, checking scores and payments on a server, and meeting Steam, Google Play, App Store or Telegram rules. This guide covers what changed this autumn, what AI handles well, where it breaks, and how to decide between doing it yourself and hiring a studio.
Methodology: this is an editorial guide. Every quote, figure and platform rule below was checked against the linked source on November 2, 2026. Where a claim has only been reported by the press and not confirmed by the company, we say so.
What changed in October 2026
Three things happened within two weeks of each other.
- Developers said games got easy. On October 28, Simon Willison, co-creator of the Django web framework and a widely read writer on AI tools, called October 2026 "a new inflection point" for vibe coding computer games. "Building games that play well is shockingly easy now," he wrote. None of his four example games took more than four hours of his own work, "plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself" (Simon Willison).
- Platforms reported a flood. PC Gamer reported that Roblox's shareholder letter says more than 500,000 users have tried Build, its prompt-to-game tool, and published over 70,000 games, and that more than 80% of the top 100 Roblox games used AI tools in the past month (PC Gamer). On itch.io, new game pages per day rose from around 3,000 to regularly over 6,000 between August 3 and October 30 (PC Gamer).
- Players pushed back. During October's Steam Next Fest, players on the Steam subreddit asked for a filter to hide games with AI-generated content (IGN). Tom's Hardware reported that Claude had started refusing to recreate specific existing games, citing a rule that reads "Don't build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." The publication noted there was no official confirmation of that text and no statement from Anthropic (Tom's Hardware).
For a business, the takeaway is not "games are free now". It is that a playable prototype is cheap, while attention, trust and polish are harder to come by than ever.
What AI does well today
- The first playable version. Willison's "Tree Appreciator", a spot-the-difference game, "required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all". His suggested starting prompt is simply "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where..." (Simon Willison).
- Browser games on known libraries. His games are HTML and JavaScript on static hosting, and he notes that frontier models "already know libraries like three.js and Phaser".
- Systems that used to need a specialist. In his strategy game Battle Drones, the soundtrack "is entirely generated through code" with no audio files, and the AI built replays and AI-versus-AI battles (Simon Willison).
- Non-programmers can get surprisingly far. A writer who set out to test whether someone who can't model, animate or code could make a 3D game built a playable browser shooter with cutscenes in about 10 days. The only paid tool was the AI coding assistant included in a $20 ChatGPT subscription, and the writer put the cost, "rounding very generously", at about $15 (Build to Understand).
Where vibe-coded games still break
The same sources that show how fast AI is also show where the time goes. These are the gaps we check first when someone sends us an AI-built game.
Sources for the table rows: Willison (October 28), Willison (October 20) and Build to Understand. The last two rows are standard engineering practice rather than findings from those posts.
Willison makes the key point himself: personal games are "the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes". A brand game is not low stakes. A broken quest in a hobby project costs nothing, while a leaderboard someone cheats in a contest with real prizes costs money and goodwill.
Platform rules for AI-made games
Steam: disclose AI content
Since January 2024, Steam's Content Survey has included an AI disclosure. It separates Pre-Generated content (art, code, sound and so on created with AI during development) from Live-Generated content (created while the game runs). For live generation you must also describe the guardrails that stop it producing illegal content, and Valve shows much of the disclosure on the store page (Valve, AI Content on Steam). The current Steamworks documentation adds that AI tools built into development environments, used for efficiency, are not the focus; the section is about AI content "that ships with your game, and is consumed by players" (Steamworks: Content Survey).
Google Play: in-app reporting for AI content
If your game generates content with AI while it runs (an AI character that chats with players, generated images or levels), Google Play requires "in-app user reporting or flagging features" so players can report offensive content without leaving the app (Google Play Console Help).
App Store: no copycats, no spam, in-app purchase for digital items
Apple's App Review Guidelines tell developers not to "simply copy the latest popular app on the App Store, or make some minor changes to another app's name or UI" (4.1 Copycats), not to flood the store with near-identical apps (4.3 Spam), and to offer "lasting entertainment value" (4.2). Game currencies, levels and premium content must be sold through in-app purchase (3.1.1) (Apple App Review Guidelines). A fast AI clone of a hit game runs into these rules even before any legal claim does.
Telegram: Stars for digital goods
Games inside Telegram must sell digital items in Telegram Stars (Telegram Stars payments). We cover the payment flow and launch options in our Telegram mini games guide.
Who owns an AI-generated game?
For a brand, this matters as much as the code. In January 2025 the US Copyright Office concluded that generative AI outputs "can be protected by copyright only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements", and that this does not include "the mere provision of prompts". Using AI to assist, or including AI material in a larger human-made work, does not by itself block protection (U.S. Copyright Office).
In practice: the more of a game's characters, writing and art comes from human creative decisions, and the better you document them, the stronger your claim to the parts that make the game yours. This is general information, not legal advice; for a campaign with a mascot or licensed brand assets, ask your lawyer.
Clones are the other side of ownership. Speaking to developers about AI-made copies, Tom Giardino of Valve's Steam business team said Valve does not want to dictate which tools studios use, and advised building a community early and continuing to improve the original, since individual mechanics are relatively easy to copy, while new features and a distinct visual style are harder to copy. He also acknowledged that building a community takes time and is not enough protection on its own (ComputerBase, in German).
Do it yourself, or hire a studio?
A prototype is never wasted. A version you have already played is a better specification than any document, and it makes a studio quote faster and more accurate.
How we use AI in our own games
We make two games of our own, Kosti, a 3D action game, and Block Nook, a block puzzle, both built in Godot 4 for Android and both still in development (see our Kosti and Block Nook project page). AI does a lot of production work in them: 3D models and rigs from text and images, concept and interface art, and voice lines in three languages. What it does not do is decide. We set the style, fix what the tools get wrong and check every asset in the engine before it ships, because the gaps in the table above are the same ones we run into.
What a studio-built game costs
Our published starting prices for games are:
- Branded Mini-Game from $8,000: advergames and playable campaigns.
- Telegram Mini App Game from $10,000: games inside Telegram with leaderboards.
- Mobile Game from $25,000: Android and iOS games, from concept to store.
"From" means the smallest sensible version; we send a fixed written quote before work starts, and new customers get 20% off the first project. If you already have a vibe-coded prototype, send it with your brief: we'll tell you what can be kept and what needs rebuilding. The full list is on our pricing page.
FAQ
Can AI make a whole game from a prompt?
For small browser games, often yes. In October 2026 Simon Willison described getting a playable spot-the-difference game from a single prompt with no follow-up. Bigger games still need iteration: his fantasy RPG needed extra playtesting and prompting to fix quest bugs, and his strategy game took 12 major iterations and 321 commits by coding agents.
Do I have to disclose AI use when I publish a game on Steam?
Yes, for AI-made content that ships with the game. Steam's Content Survey asks you to describe AI content created during development (Pre-Generated) and AI content created while the game runs (Live-Generated), and Valve shows much of that disclosure on the store page. Valve says AI coding tools used for efficiency are not the focus of that section.
Do I own the copyright in an AI-generated game?
In the US, only partly. The Copyright Office concluded in January 2025 that AI outputs are protected only where a human author determined sufficient expressive elements, and that prompts alone are not enough. Human-made art, writing and creative changes to AI output can be protected. For a brand game, get legal advice and keep a record of the human work.
When is a vibe-coded game good enough for a brand campaign?
When nothing valuable rides on it: an internal demo, a pitch prototype or a short single-player toy with no prizes, no personal data and no payments. Once there are real prizes, a leaderboard people will try to cheat, sign-ups, purchases or a store release, the parts AI tools skip (server checks, testing on real phones, store rules and support) need engineering.
Building inside Telegram? Read our Telegram mini games guide. Built an app (not a game) with AI? See how to make an AI-built app production-ready.
Have a game idea or an AI prototype? Get a fixed quote.
Send us the prototype or a short brief. We reply within one business day with a fixed written quote: Branded Mini-Game from $8,000, Telegram Mini App Game from $10,000, Mobile Game from $25,000. New customers get 20% off the first project.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
articles.body:
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Whether you intend to put its many tracking features to the test, or you simply want the longest battery life of any Apple Watch, it’s currently on sale for $699.99 ($100 off) in multiple colors at Amazon, matching its all-time low price.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $100 off, matching its best price to date
We also found a good deal on Ugreen’s soccer ball-shaped Bluetooth tracker with seven years of battery life.
Powered by Apple’s new S11 chip (also in the Series 12), the Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers faster performance than the last-gen version, plus a handful of new Apple Intelligence features. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. An upcoming Siri Recap feature will be able to create summaries of conversations for later reference.
This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy.
On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist.
Three more ways to save
- Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items.
- If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off).
- Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. The versatile tool can help with repairing stuff, or putting together decorations. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it. The stapler comes with 1,200 fasteners.

articles.title: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
articles.body:
Apple’s latest earnings show how it’s continuing to capitalize on the AI boom without busting its budget on the infrastructure spending consuming its competitors.
Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
AI was mentioned 45 times on the quarterly earnings call.
Overall, Apple posted its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone and Mac sales continued to grow strongly in the fourth quarter. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares nevertheless fell in premarket trading Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze its profit margins in the holiday quarter.
Apple hasn’t disclosed how much of its revenue growth reflects AI demand or higher prices, but its executives clearly see the technology as a way to drive further sales.
During the earnings call, CFO Kevan Parekh cited a “wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time.”
“On the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities,” he said. “And we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.”
Apple can sell its giant user base the devices they use for AI, even if the AI itself comes from someone else. It can collect fees on subscriptions to AI apps. And it can charge customers who want more access to its own AI features.
“We see tremendous opportunity in AI,” John Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.
AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the earnings call, according to financial research platform AlphaSense — even more than on the call following Apple’s unveiling of the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.
Mentions of AI or “Apple Intelligence” on earnings calls
On the call, Apple continued to position itself as the interface through which consumers use AI — including competitors’ technology. With more than 2.5 billion active devices, it already has an enormous audience for whatever AI services emerge.
Apple, unlike its Big Tech peers, isn’t pouring comparable sums into infrastructure. Its approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology. Siri AI uses models developed with Google’s Gemini technology while Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation.
Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon’s $77.3 billion and Alphabet’s $51.4 billion. Those totals cover companywide CapEx, not just AI, and exclude some AI expenses. Apple’s operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased R&D spending, including on AI. Siri AI’s cloud costs will appear in services cost of sales. Those costs could grow with usage: Parekh said it’s too early to predict how many requests will require servers rather than on-device processing. Still, Apple’s capital spending remains just a fraction of its peers’.
More AI usage also gives Apple something to sell.
Siri AI is only beginning to reach customers. Apple launched the revamped assistant in beta for US English users in September and expanded it to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Apple plans to turn some of that usage into subscription revenue. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits. Customers who need more capacity “will be able to purchase expanded access in the future,” he said. “In the beginning, iCloud tiers were largely about storage, but we’ve been adding more capabilities and features to it.”
Apple also benefits when customers buy its hardware to run AI locally, including models developed by other companies. Mac, Ternus said, is “having an AI moment all its own.”
“We feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities.”
Apple offered specific examples of companies putting its computers to work on AI. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, avoiding cloud token costs for those tasks. Christie’s is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates.
For those customers, buying Apple hardware provides a way to use AI without paying a cloud provider for every request.
Mac Mini and Mac Studio, Ternus said, “are pushing the boundaries of local, private AI, giving users the ability to do things once considered impossible.”
The Mac Mini’s emergence as an AI machine has given the small, screenless desktop a new constituency among developers and hobbyists looking for a relatively affordable way to run models locally. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio’s capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.
Apple also makes money when customers subscribe to someone else’s AI. Earlier this year, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to analytics firm AppMagic.
That revenue, of course, depends on customers paying through Apple’s system. OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead of the App Store, bypassing Apple’s commissions, The Wall Street Journal reported. Apple’s position gives it a way to profit from competitors’ AI, but those competitors have an incentive to find a route around its fees.
Still, Apple already has multiple ways to benefit from people using AI. It can sell the computer, collect a subscription commission, and eventually charge for more of its own services. It doesn’t have to build every model — or fund infrastructure on its competitors’ scale — to get paid.

articles.title: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads
articles.body:
Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house.
About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Intel (INTC) led the way down again.
The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended.
And the damage didn't stick to Intel.
Micron (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), Seagate (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell (MRVL) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum (LITE) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia (NVDA) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6.
Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants.
Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX (SPCX) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet (FTNT) and CrowdStrike (CRWD), which fell with chips.
Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst.
"The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom."
John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening.
"There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia."
Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term "Octoberphobia," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%.
Next up is AMD (AMD), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell, the same day as the midterm vote.

articles.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
articles.body:
The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public
Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026
Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts.
Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings, extensive use of financial engineering, and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies.
That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut.
The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is.
Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer.
Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due.
The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models.
Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense: they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so.
Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts, Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments.
Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic.
Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins
First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies, including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%).
Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid.
Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential.
In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required.
That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion, and the prices for some components are soaring.
That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments.
And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task.
Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher.
Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost.
If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice.
It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect.” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches.
The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy.

articles.title: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
articles.body:
Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week, shares tumbled 8.8% Monday.
"This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it."
Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments.
The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion.
"This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday.
Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028.
Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%.
The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan.
While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes.
What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday.
"Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."
— CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

articles.title: Monsters of Ohio is OUT!!!
articles.body:
Monsters of Ohio is OUT!!!
Posted on November 3, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 9 Comments
It’s time! Monsters of Ohio is out in the world, available at your favorite bookseller in print and ebook, and also in audio through Audible. In the UK, it will be available on the 5th, because that’s just when books get put out over there. Here are links for Amazon, Barnes & Noble, Bookshop and of course it’s available just about everywhere else as well, including your own local bookstore.
MOO (as it rather delightfully initializes down to) has gotten great reviews, including starred reviews in Bookpage, Kirkus and Library Journal, which makes me happy. It’s also a Library Reads Hall of Fame pick, which also delights me.
Also, I’m on a book tour — starting today! — through (mostly) the American Midwest, because it seemed the right place to tour this particular book. Please come see me and support the booksellers hosting me this time around.
Not on my tour schedule but still want a signed copy? You can order a copy from any one of the bookstores hosting me on my tour and I will be happy to sign the book while I am in their shop so they can ship it to you. I will also be signing copies for my own local bookstore, Jay & Mary’s Book Center, today, so they will have signed copies available as well. All of those are likely to ship only to the US, sorry.
(Also we’ll be announcing our annual holiday signing thing tomorrow, so stay tuned for that!)
Monsters of Ohio takes place, as the title suggests, in Ohio — but more than that, it takes place where I live, in the fictional town of Richland, located in the very real Darke County. Lots of elements of the book are taken from or inspired by my immediate surroundings, and in many ways this is the most personal novel I’ve written, and certainly the novel closest to me in a geographical sense. Now, it also has monsters and exploding things, so there’s that too. There’s a lot going on here.
The point is, I’m really proud of this one. I hope you all like it.
Also, in the US it’s election day. If you’ve not done so already, vote! And then get this book as a reward. If every voter in the United States rewarded themselves with this book, then, well. It would be a very good day for me.
— JS

articles.title: Snap settles lawsuit accusing platform of fueling teen depression and eating disorders
articles.body:
Snap has reached a settlement in a lawsuit brought by two teenagers who accused the company of designing its platform to be addictive and contributing to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders, as first reported by Reuters. The plaintiffs had previously reached settlements with Meta, TikTok, and YouTube.
The trial was set to be Snap’s first in a broader wave of litigation over social media’s impact on young users. The company had already settled its other cases scheduled for trial. Snap CEO Evan Spiegel was expected to take the stand.
The plaintiffs said they started using YouTube as young as age 3 and other social media platforms at around age 9. They said they developed compulsive usage habits, which they attributed to features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling.
“The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community.”
Social media giants are facing thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims that they knowingly designed their platforms to hook young users and fuel a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression, and suicide.

articles.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
articles.body:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:
						
Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day
I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.
Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.
I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit, I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.
I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:
						
I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!
Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it.
I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.
Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.
Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.
I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.
But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.
It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

articles.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
articles.body:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:
						
Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day
I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.

articles.title: Can’t fish Ethernet? Use “invisible” fiber instead
articles.body:
My family owns a NYC townhouse, and with that I had Cat6 cables put in on each floor.
However, more recently, one of the Cat6 cables has gone “bad,” meaning it only does 100 Mbps. While we are nowhere close to Gigabit speeds, very less multi-Gig (despite me having had symmetric Gigabit in the past), it’s still not something I’m happy about.
What do you mean only 100 Mbps? My switch and AP support 2.5 Gbps.
The most common approaches in my scenario are:
- Fish a new cable
- Abandon the cable and use wireless mesh
However, there are a few issues:
- The cables were fished in a funky way, and considering how clumsy I am I don’t want to cause more damage
- Our walls are thick, meaning wireless mesh would suck
When I did use mesh on HPE AP25s (the APs I use), the performance was 120 Mbps at two prior homes, that with thin walls and fiber. I also want VLAN segmentation so a typical consumer Eero or Orbi won’t work.
So what did I do? “Invisible” fiber between two floors.
In case you didn’t know, there are special types of fiber cables originally designed for apartment retrofits. This is to avoid landlord/HOA complaints. Our prior place had Verizon Fios via these cables in the hallway.
But these cables are also sold on Amazon and AliExpress for people who’re in rentals or don’t want to fish cables.
So how did I do it?
Galore, the endpoints of my 20m/60ft ‘fiber in the home’ loop.
Switch
While there are SFP+ switches, I already had an unused MikroTik CRS304-4XG-IN, so I just used it here. It’s technically copper 10G, but I’d lose more by trading it for a SFP+ switch so I’ll just keep it. Not to mention copper SFP+s get hot.
Media Converters and Transceivers
I used two media converters and a pair of bidirectional SC SFP+s.
The SFP+s use the same SC connector used in PON networks, but otherwise use Active Ethernet. I’m not sure if they’re using IEEE standards or are proprietary on the glass, but I’ll assume the latter.
While there’s copper on the media converters, the other option would be to replace our switch which I’ve mentioned is not the best idea.
The Fiber
While the fiber can (and is designed to) be superglued, I chose to use the included adhesive instead. Why? In case I ever have to remove it, which has happened before.
That’s the same reason why I did the basement AP25 using command strips when everyone else just drills the mount.
While our fiber is UPC, our transceivers support both SC fiber types.
Conclusion
If I look at the Instant On portal, I’m posting this from my MacBook connected to the new ‘fiber in the home’ loop (via an HPE AP25).
While we currently lack fiber-to-the-home (Mamdani, please fix Fios rights of way!), I’m still happy I could DIY a fix for a Cat6 cable with bad pairs.
In fact, while I don’t have multi-Gig I could still get a respectable ~300 Mbps:
So yes, even if you don’t have fiber to the home, fiber is still useful in a home network. As it saved me from having to hire a contractor and possibly tear our walls. Not to mention a $1500 Samsung TV is on the wall the “defective” Cat6 cable is behind.

articles.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
articles.body:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 27 Oct 2026]
Title:Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at this https URL.

articles.title: Skill to Create Product Videos
articles.body:
From product workflow to polished demo.
v1.0.1 release · aaitor/skill-video-studio
Quick start · Worked videos · Usage · Contribute
A local video-production workspace driven by the /devrel-video Claude Code skill. Capture real product interactions with Playwright CLI, compose title cards, chapters, and CTAs with HyperFrames, then master and inspect the result with FFmpeg. Start with a silent walkthrough; add narration, music, subtitles, or your own presenter footage when needed.
A real Claude Code session using the installed project skill: clone the studio, prepare an Acme walkthrough brief, and inspect the three-beat plan on a black background. This short demo stops before capture and rendering; it does not claim a video was produced. The recording guide includes the actual generated brief and reproduction command.
For planning: Git and authenticated Claude Code. Clone the full workspace so its native skill and project layout stay together:
git clone https://github.com/aaitor/skill-video-studio.git
cd skill-video-studio
claude
Ask Claude:
/devrel-video Prepare a 25-second silent walkthrough brief for the bundled
Acme app: show the workspace, filter by category, then open a project.
Reuse brands/acme. Show the plan before capture or rendering.
Expected result: a project brief and a concrete beat plan. For a complete video, install the capture/render prerequisites and follow the worked walkthrough. The production stack needs Node.js 22+, FFmpeg/ffprobe, Chromium, and the helper-specific Python dependencies. Optional narration and avatars require your own additional services or GPU setup.
- Real product capture: browser interaction scripts with explicit beats and stable selectors.
- Branded composition: title, browser frame, chapters, and CTA in a HyperFrames timeline.
- Local mastering and QA: master/web copies, ffprobe checks, contact sheet, and thumbnail.
- Optional audio: six local music styles, narration-driven timing, and voice variants.
- Optional presentation: subtitles, private bring-your-own presenter footage, and terminal/browser sequences.
- Source-based workflow: reusable brands, briefs, templates, and two complete worked examples.
Portrait/social output profiles remain on the roadmap. Full capture/render depends on your local toolchain; offline CI checks sources and selected local utilities, not the complete production stack. See workflow and usage.
Product walkthrough: a local Acme fixture, real browser capture, narration/music, and EN/ES subtitles. Source and commands · Watch with sound.
Composed CLI/browser film: a multi-environment example whose terminal scenes are authored HTML reenactments. Source and explanation · Watch with sound.
The longer examples remain intact. Generated MP4/audio files are ignored; rebuild them from the included sources. See usage prompts for silent, narrated, avatar, voice-swap, and multi-environment requests.
Each video uses projects/<slug>/brief.yaml, brand tokens under brands/<name>/, and generated output under its project folder. Optional private settings live outside Git, selected by DEVREL_VIDEO_ENV.
See configuration, the actual brief template, and security/privacy guidance. Keep private footage and credentials outside this public repository.
Brief → explore → brand → capture → compose → optional layers → render/QA → thumbnail. The skill coordinates existing tools rather than replacing them. Detailed production steps are in the workflow guide and production notes.
.claude/skills/devrel-video/  Skill instructions, scripts, templates, production notes
brands/                     Brand tokens and logos
projects/                   Curated public examples; private projects stay ignored
examples/                   Real harness recording, public input, generated brief
assets/                     Shared banner, social card, and short terminal GIF
docs/                       Onboarding, usage, configuration, troubleshooting
- Installation and production prerequisites
- Configuration
- Prompts and optional layers
- Workflow
- Troubleshooting
- Security, privacy, and media rights
- Banner generation and social preview
- Original references: studio design guide · avatar guide
Use Issues for questions, bugs, and ideas. Read CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md; report vulnerabilities privately through SECURITY.md.
Install requirements-dev.txt in a virtual environment and run python3 scripts/check.py. See CHANGELOG.md for changes. Live recordings, service calls, GPU jobs, and full renders are manual validation steps.
MIT for original studio content. Embedded banner fonts retain their OFL notices; external tools/models/media retain their own terms. See licensing.

articles.title: One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
articles.body:
Google says one of its Android manufacturing partners secretly built a backdoor in 1.3 million devices and turned them into a botnet. The company says it has now dismantled the backdoor and “cut ties” with the manufacturer, the Shenzhen, China-based Videostrong Technology Co., which has been banned from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software for them.
One of Google’s Android partners turned 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet
Google says a manufacturer ‘intentionally’ hijacked its devices with malware.
The infected devices were used without owners’ knowledge for “malicious activity,” like ad fraud, data exfiltration, and routing unauthorized network traffic. Google claims the “backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain,” saying:
Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
It wasn’t just one device that was impacted, either — the malware was found “built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years.” Most of those were Android TV set-top boxes, but the botnet also infected other “Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.”
Google says Videostrong used “obfuscation techniques” to load the malware onto users’ devices after they booted up the hardware for the first time. Google also says it made changes to its review process for device manufacturers after this incident.

articles.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
articles.body:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.
On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.
Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.
Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.
Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.
In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.
Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.
That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish.
Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content.
Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system.
Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder.
Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear.
Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel
articles.body:
Bethesda is officially confirming today that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI Sentinel. The confirmation came in a less than 10-minute video celebrating 40 years of Bethesda game studios.
The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel
Bethesda celebrates 40 years with a fresh Elder Scrolls VI teaser.
It’s been more than eight years since Bethesda officially announced the existence of the sixth game in its Elder Scrolls series, and studio chief Todd Howard made the announcement today and called it the “perfect time” to fully name the game.
Bethesda isn’t sharing any more details on The Elder Scrolls VI Sentinel today, though. The Xbox Wire press release on the name is literally just a picture of the logo.
I reported in Notepad last week that Bethesda was planning to name the game in November, during a period that will mark 15 years since The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim was released. Sentinel will be set in Hammerfell, a province in the Elder Scrolls universe that’s appeared in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online. Sentinel will be the first game about the history of the Elder Scrolls, and help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts.

articles.title: Adobe’s Premiere mobile app is adding licensed music from ‘leading artists’
articles.body:
Adobe is teaming up with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group to add a library of licensed music clips to the Premiere mobile video editing app. No specific musicians have been announced with this partnership, but Adobe said it will include “popular songs” from “leading artists,” and enable Premiere mobile users to quickly jump on “the latest trend.”
Adobe’s Premiere mobile app is adding licensed music from ‘leading artists’
Universal and Warner music groups are working with Adobe to provide a browsable library of fully licensed song clips.
“By bringing licensed music from UMG artists into Adobe Premiere mobile, we’re giving creators new ways to build their stories around the songs they love for the first time, while helping our artists and songwriters reach new audiences,” Universal Music Group’s Bryan Stone said in the announcement.
Adobe says this feature is “coming soon,” and will allow Premiere mobile users to:
- Add up to 60 seconds of a popular track directly to the video.
- Browse, search and preview trending music by artist or track, filter by genre and duration, bookmark favorites, and explore popular music through label-featured collections.
- Access customizable templates that are already paired with music to speed up editing.
- Export finished videos in Premiere mobile and post to licensed social platforms.
The Premiere Pro desktop app and Premiere mobile both already include a built-in library of royalty-free music that editors can work into their videos, but licensed audio needs to be manually imported. This update aims to make it easier to incorporate recognizable music into video edits, and help Adobe’s mobile video editor compete against popular rivals like CapCut. We have asked Adobe if these updates will also be coming to Premiere Pro, and will update if we hear back.
